paragraphs: It is explained in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot, Parashat Ekev, that you should have intention throughout the time of your eating, and at the very least when you eat that olive-sized piece over which the berachah of HaMotzi was said — a brief intention in general terms, and it is this: the matter of extraction (birur) is accomplished through the thirty-two teeth, which correspond to the thirty-two Netivot Chochmah (Paths of Wisdom) that extract everything, for in thought all is extracted; they grind and crumble the food, and through this the edible part is extracted from the waste, the way millstones grind grain, and afterward the bran and husks — which are the kelipot (husks) — are separated from the flour, which is the food, which was not the case before it was ground, when they were bound together completely — end of his wording. And it is further written there that one should have intention regarding two aspects of extraction in the food one eats: the first is the extraction of the food itself, of its good part, from the dross mixed into it through the sin of Adam HaRishon, and also what was mixed into it from the beginning of its creation during the six days of Creation; and the second is the matter of the rectification of reincarnated souls (nefashot hamegulgalim) found in food and drink — see there. It is further written there, in his own words: you should have the intention of swallowing the food after it has been chewed, for it is there, in the stomach, that the extraction is completed, for then the food is digested and its good part turns into blood, and the nourishment goes to the liver and spreads through all the veins and organs, as is known, while the bad part of it descends through the intestines and exits outward — end of his wording. And all these intentions are simple and are very necessary even for a simple person, and every literate person should accustom himself to them. And in the holy work Makbetzi'el I wrote: although our teacher, of blessed memory, wrote that the extraction must be through thirty-two teeth corresponding to the Netivot Chochmah, and repeated this matter two or three times in his words in Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot — nevertheless, if a person is found whose teeth have fallen out and only four or six remain to him, do not think that the rectification mentioned is thereby deficient; rather, even with this small remainder he accomplishes the complete rectification, since he originally had thirty-two teeth, and this remainder comes by way of a portion of the thirty-two Netivot Chochmah. An analogy to this you will find in the law of washing the hands, where the water purifies through 'remnants of purity' (shiyurei taharah), since they come from a complete measure, as mentioned in Shulchan Aruch, siman 160, se'if 13, where some permit even when people wash one after another and so on — that whoever [the remaining water reaches] came from remnants of purity — see there.

clarification.explanation: The Ari wrote that one should have the intention of extraction (birur) at the time of eating: the extraction is accomplished through the thirty-two teeth, which correspond to the thirty-two Paths of Wisdom, which grind and separate the food from the waste like millstones separating bran from flour. One should have intention regarding two extractions: the extraction of the food itself from the dross mixed into it from the sin of Adam HaRishon and from the six days of Creation, and the rectification of reincarnated souls found in food and drink. Upon swallowing, when the food reaches the stomach, the extraction is completed: the good turns into blood and nourishes the body, and the bad exits through the intestines. These intentions are simple, and every literate person should accustom himself to them, or at least have this intention with the piece of HaMotzi. And one whose teeth have fallen out and few remain should not think the rectification is lacking, since even the small remainder — coming as it does from the power of the thirty-two Paths — accomplishes the rectification in full.
takeaways: At the time of eating, one has intention of extracting the good from the waste (thirty-two teeth corresponding to the thirty-two Paths)
Even one with few remaining teeth accomplishes the rectification in full

paragraphs: Those leftover bits of food carried on bones and on fruit peels — if they contain sparks of holiness — are extracted through the final berachah that a person recites at his table, even though they will ultimately be thrown into the trash. Therefore a person should be careful not to remove bones and peels from the table except after Birkat HaMazon, as the Kabbalists wrote, and so it is written in Chesed LaAlafim, siman 180, ot alef. And for this reason we have heard a warning that one should not take anything from the table to feed to non-kosher domestic animals, beasts, or fowl before Birkat HaMazon, as mentioned there. And those people whose custom is to eat cooked meat dishes first, and after their eating bring fruit to the table — for whom it is difficult to place the fruit dishes while the table is scattered with meat bones and the like — there is a remedy for this: they should spread another tablecloth over the table so that the bones and remains of the cooked dishes are covered, and arrange the fruit dishes to come on the clean tablecloth; it then turns out that they recite Birkat HaMazon while the bones and peels are still on the table, and thereby their extraction is completed.

clarification.explanation: Leftover bits of food remaining on bones and on fruit peels — if they contain sparks of holiness, they are extracted through the final berachah a person recites at his table, even though they will ultimately be thrown into the trash. Therefore one should be careful not to remove bones and peels from the table except after Birkat HaMazon (as the Kabbalists wrote, and Chesed LaAlafim). For this reason, one also should not take anything from the table to feed to non-kosher domestic animals, beasts, or fowl before Birkat HaMazon. And those whose custom is to eat meat dishes first and then bring fruit, who find it difficult to place the fruit dishes on a table scattered with bones and mess — there is a remedy for this: spread another tablecloth over the table to cover the bones and remains of the cooked dishes, and arrange the fruit dishes on the clean tablecloth; thus they recite Birkat HaMazon while the bones and peels are still on the table, and their extraction is thereby completed.
takeaways: Bones and peels are not removed from the table until after Birkat HaMazon — the berachah extracts the sparks of holiness within them.
One likewise should not take food from the table to feed non-kosher animals or fowl before Birkat HaMazon.
If the table is messy, spread a clean tablecloth over it and arrange the fruit on top, leaving the bones underneath until Birkat HaMazon.

paragraphs: Since Birkat HaMazon effects a great rectification upon the table, as mentioned, our Sages therefore warned that a person should leave bread on his table at the time of Birkat HaMazon, and in the holy Zohar this was treated stringently, and they based it on the verse, "You shall not take the Name of the Lord your God in vain" (Shemot 20:7). And if they ate all the bread before Birkat HaMazon and did not notice until the time of Birkat HaMazon, they should not bring a whole loaf and place it on the table, but should bring a slice; and if there was a whole loaf on the table from the time HaMotzi was recited, one should not remove it at the time of Birkat HaMazon — indeed it is preferable to do so, to leave one whole loaf on the table from the time HaMotzi was recited. And they only prohibited a whole loaf when one brings it anew at the time of Birkat HaMazon.

clarification.explanation: Since Birkat HaMazon effects a great rectification upon the table, our Sages warned to leave bread on the table during the berachah, and the Zohar treated this stringently, basing it on the verse "You shall not take the Name of the Lord your God in vain." If they ate all the bread and did not notice until the time of the berachah, they should not bring a whole loaf but rather a slice. And if there was a whole loaf on the table from the time of HaMotzi, one should not remove it — indeed it is preferable to leave a whole loaf there from the time of HaMotzi; a whole loaf was only prohibited when brought anew at the time of Birkat HaMazon.
takeaways: Bread is left on the table during Birkat HaMazon
If all was eaten, bring a slice; but a whole loaf that was already there from the start is not removed

paragraphs: One must be careful that no empty vessel remain on the table at the time of Birkat HaMazon, such as spoons, cups, and bowls and the like; one must also be careful not to leave a knife on the table at the time of Birkat HaMazon.

clarification.explanation: One must be careful that no empty vessel remain on the table at the time of Birkat HaMazon, such as spoons, cups, and bowls, and one must likewise be careful not to leave a knife on the table during the berachah.
takeaways: No empty vessel is left on the table during Birkat HaMazon
No knife is left on the table during the berachah

paragraphs: It is forbidden to waste crumbs that contain an olive's-bulk (kezayit); therefore one should be careful that drops of water from the netilat yadayim (handwashing) not fall onto crumbs on the table, for they would thereby become repulsive. And even crumbs that do not contain a kezayit, it is forbidden to waste and make them repulsive, for this brings hardship of poverty, God forbid, even over a small matter. And this warning applies especially to women, who are found in the home and whose eyes should constantly be scanning the floor of the house for this reason; and a woman of valor should always sweep the eating area with her own hands after the meal and throw the crumbs into the oven, and should not rely on the servant, and of her it is said (Mishlei 31:11), "Her husband's heart trusts in her, and he shall lack no gain." And for this our Sages said (Bava Metzia 59a): blessing is found in a person's house only for the sake of his wife — because she watches to make sure not to waste small crumbs, and then her husband shall lack no gain, for his bread shall not be lacking. And they should be careful to shake out the tablecloth into the oven; and on Friday night they should shake it out in a place designated for this, and after Shabbat they should sweep the place where they shook it and throw [the crumbs] into the oven. And likewise the woman should be careful to sweep the place where the bread is stored and to sweep it and throw [the crumbs] into the oven, since there are necessarily crumbs there at the time of putting bread in and taking it out. And likewise bread sellers in the market should be careful to sweep around the bin from which they sell the bread, since many crumbs fall when they take bread out of it to weigh for the buyers, and they should throw the dust together with the crumbs in it into the oven. And this warning is needed especially here in our towns, where the bread is light and not so thick, since it is not made in the [furan-style oven] (an oven built with a raised surface, with its opening on the side), (in Arabic, tzamun — a round, puffy loaf of bread), and therefore many more crumbs fall from it than from bread baked in the furan; therefore the masses of the people must be warned about this, and especially regarding wafers (rekikin), from which it is impossible that crumbs not fall.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to waste crumbs containing a kezayit, and therefore one should be careful that water drops from netilat yadayim not fall on the crumbs on the table and make them repulsive. And even crumbs that do not contain a kezayit, it is forbidden to waste and make them repulsive, for this brings hardship of poverty even over a small matter. This warning applies especially to women who are found in the home, and a woman of valor should always sweep the eating area with her own hands and throw the crumbs into the oven, and not rely on the servant; of her it is said, "Her husband's heart trusts in her, and he shall lack no gain." One should shake out the tablecloth into the oven (on Shabbat night, in a designated place, and afterward sweep and throw into the oven), and sweep the place where the bread is stored. Likewise bread sellers in the market should sweep around the place of sale and throw the crumbs into the oven. This warning is especially needed where the bread is light and soft and sheds many crumbs, and particularly with wafers.
takeaways: It is forbidden to waste crumbs, and certainly a kezayit; one should not let handwashing water drip onto them
Women and bread sellers should be careful to sweep the eating area and bread storage/sale area and throw the crumbs into the oven

paragraphs: Before Birkat HaMazon one should be careful to take mayim acharonim (the final handwashing) into a vessel, for mayim acharonim is obligatory even if one ate only bread, since there is a great reason for it according to the holy Zohar and the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot, Parashat Ekev. And it is written there that at the time of taking mayim acharonim, one should join the four fingers together separately and the thumb separately, and lower one's fingers downward.

clarification.explanation: Before Birkat HaMazon one should be careful to take mayim acharonim into a vessel, since mayim acharonim is obligatory even if one ate only bread, and it has a great reason according to the Zohar and the Ari. At the time of taking it, one should join the four fingers together separately and the thumb separately, and lower the fingers downward.
takeaways: Mayim acharonim is obligatory even when one ate only bread, taken into a vessel
Join the four fingers together and the thumb separately, fingers pointed downward

paragraphs: In the statement of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, mentioned above, that mayim acharonim is obligatory, several secret intentions of mayim acharonim are hinted at. Therefore it is good that before a person extends his hand to take mayim acharonim, he should state this halachah: "Mayim acharonim is obligatory." And I heard from the crown of my head, my father, of blessed memory, that it was the custom of the crown of his head, my master and grandfather, Rabbeinu Moshe Chaim, of blessed memory, to say this halachah before taking mayim acharonim, and sometimes he relied on this halachah in place of words of Torah that are said at the table before Birkat HaMazon, when there was no time to say words of Torah, since this is a halachah from the Oral Torah, and a thing said in its proper time is good indeed.

clarification.explanation: In the Sages' statement "mayim acharonim is obligatory" several secret intentions are hinted, and therefore it is good that before extending one's hand to take mayim acharonim, one should say this halachah, "mayim acharonim is obligatory." This was likewise the custom of Rabbeinu's grandfather, and at times he relied on saying this halachah in place of words of Torah said at the table before Birkat HaMazon when there was no time, since this is a halachah of the Oral Torah.
takeaways: It is good to say "mayim acharonim is obligatory" before taking it, since intentions are hinted within it
This halachah can serve as words of Torah at the table when there is no time

paragraphs: One should be careful that the mayim acharonim be little, and not use much of it, for it is the portion of the Sitra Achra (the Other Side). And if one's hands are very soiled from the cooked dish, and likewise one's mouth and mustache, requiring much water to wash them, it is good to wash them before taking mayim acharonim with the intention of continuing to eat afterward, and let these be like "intermediate water" (mayim emtza'im); and one should do so: after washing them, one should eat a piece of bread from the table so that this washing not be considered mayim acharonim, and after eating the piece of bread and the like, one should take a small amount of mayim acharonim and recite Birkat HaMazon — see Kaf HaChaim, siman 25, ot bet.

clarification.explanation: One should be careful that the mayim acharonim be little and not use much of it, since it is the portion of the Sitra Achra. And if one's hands are very soiled from the cooked dish, and likewise the mouth and mustache requiring much water, it is good to wash them beforehand with the intention of continuing to eat, and these count as "intermediate water"; after washing, one should eat a piece of bread so that this washing not be counted as mayim acharonim, and then take a small amount of mayim acharonim and recite the berachah.
takeaways: Mayim acharonim should be little, as it is the portion of the Sitra Achra
For very soiled hands: wash first as "intermediate water," eat bread, then take a small amount of mayim acharonim

paragraphs: The later authorities wrote in the name of the Kabbalists, of blessed memory, that when one takes mayim acharonim he should say, "This is the portion of a wicked man from God" (Iyov 20:29), and should have intention that "chelek adam rasha" (portion of a wicked man) is an acrostic for "achar" (other), which is the Sitra Achra — see Kaf HaChaim. And I wrote in the holy work Makbetzi'el that one who follows this practice should say these words in a whisper, and the wise will understand.

clarification.explanation: The later authorities wrote in the name of the Kabbalists that when taking mayim acharonim one should say, "This is the portion of a wicked man from God," with the intention that "chelek adam rasha" is an acrostic for "achar" (the Sitra Achra). One who follows this practice should say these words in a whisper.
takeaways: It is customary to say "This is the portion of a wicked man from God" during mayim acharonim
And to say it in a whisper

paragraphs: One does not take mayim acharonim directly onto the ground, but into a vessel; and if no vessel can be found, one should take it onto wood or onto the floor, since no evil spirit rests upon a floor as it rests upon bare ground. And mayim emtza'im (intermediate water), which is taken between eating dairy and meat, likewise requires a vessel.

clarification.explanation: One does not take mayim acharonim onto the ground but into a vessel. If no vessel can be found, one should take it onto wood or onto the floor, since no evil spirit rests upon a floor as it does upon bare ground. And mayim emtza'im, taken between eating dairy and meat, likewise requires a vessel.
takeaways: Mayim acharonim into a vessel; if none available, onto wood or floor, not bare ground
Mayim emtza'im (between dairy and meat) likewise requires a vessel

paragraphs: One does not take with hot water that the hand would be scalded by, and some say it must be actually cold, and it is proper to be careful about this; and some say it must be fit for drinking, that it not be bitter or foul-smelling; it must also come by human effort. And if one transgressed and did not take mayim acharonim, he should take it after Birkat HaMazon; and if he has no water, he should take with some other beverage, even wine, since he has no other way to take it.

clarification.explanation: One does not take mayim acharonim with water hot enough to scald the hand, and some say it must be actually cold, and it is proper to be careful about this. Some say it must be fit for drinking — not bitter or foul-smelling — and must come by human effort. If one forgot and did not take mayim acharonim, he should take it after Birkat HaMazon; and if he has no water, he may use another beverage, even wine, since he has no other way.
takeaways: The water should not be too hot, and it is proper that it be cold and fit for drinking
If one forgot: take it after the berachah; if no water is available, use another beverage

paragraphs: One must take up to the joint of the fingers, so the early authorities, of blessed memory, wrote; and it appears to me that one must take up to the third joint, the beginning of the third joint included, for so it appears from the language of Rabbeinu HaRash"ash, of blessed memory, in his siddur, where he wrote to have intention in taking [mayim acharonim] regarding the fourteen joints of the right [hand] and so on — see there — implying that the taking is for fourteen joints, and this seems correct.

clarification.explanation: One must take mayim acharonim up to the joint of the fingers. In Rabbeinu's view, one must take up to and including the third joint, since it appears from the wording of the HaRash"ash in his siddur, who wrote to have intention in the taking regarding the fourteen joints of the hand, implying that the taking covers all fourteen joints.
takeaways: Mayim acharonim is taken up to the joint of the fingers
In Rabbeinu's view, up to and including the third joint (fourteen joints)

paragraphs: One who measures salt or touches salt is obligated to wash his hands afterward; and likewise even without a meal, when eating cucumbers and similar things which people typically put salt on with their fingers, one must wash his hands afterward, for even though Sodomite salt is not commonly found, one should be concerned about a type of salt whose nature is like Sodomite salt, and every person should be concerned for himself to fulfill the words of the Sages — see Chesed LaAlafim and other later authorities.

clarification.explanation: One who measures salt or touches salt must wash his hands afterward. Likewise, even without a formal meal, when eating cucumbers and similar things that people typically salt with their fingers, one must wash his hands afterward, since although Sodomite salt is not commonly found, one should be concerned about a type of salt whose nature resembles it (which blinds the eyes), and every person should be concerned for himself to fulfill the words of the Sages.
takeaways: One who touches salt washes his hands afterward, out of concern for salt resembling Sodomite salt
This applies even outside a meal, when touching salt with one's fingers

paragraphs: There is one who says that if one ate a moist food such that his hands become soiled by it, then by strict law, when he washes his hands he should recite the berachah "al netilat yadayim" (regarding the washing of hands); but the world has not adopted the practice of reciting this berachah, even though those who require this berachah are great authorities of the world, for we hold that in cases of doubt regarding berachot, we are lenient; nevertheless, every person should have this berachah in mind in his heart.

clarification.explanation: There is an opinion that if one ate a moist food that soiled his hands, then by strict law he should recite "al netilat yadayim" when washing his hands afterward. But the common practice is not to recite this berachah, even though the great authorities who require it are significant, since we hold that in cases of doubt regarding berachot we are lenient; nevertheless, every person should have this berachah in mind in his heart.
takeaways: Some hold one should recite "al netilat yadayim" after a moist food, but common practice does not, since doubtful berachot are treated leniently
One should have the berachah in mind in his heart

paragraphs: One must be careful not to interrupt between mayim acharonim and Birkat HaMazon even with words of Torah, and one should say only these verses after the mayim acharonim, before Birkat HaMazon: the entire psalm "Elohim Yechoneinu Vivarcheinu" (God shall be gracious to us and bless us), and it is good to visualize in one's mind the shape of the Menorah; and after it one should say "Avarechah et Hashem bechol et" and so on, with the intention of driving away the Sitra Achra standing at the table; and after it, the verse "Sof davar hakol nishma" and so on, and the verse "Tehillat Hashem yedaber pi" and so on, and the verse "Va'anachnu nevarech Kah me'atah ve'ad olam, Halleluyah," and afterward "Vayedaber elai: zeh hashulchan asher lifnei Hashem," with intention regarding the final letters of the words "zeh-hashulchan-asher," which allude to "NaHaR" (river). And he should recite Birkat HaMazon with eyes closed, as in the Amidah prayer, placing the left hand against the chest and the right hand upon the left, and reciting the berachah with intention, since the Sitra Achra stands there to accuse him if he does not recite the berachah with intention.

clarification.explanation: One must be careful not to interrupt between mayim acharonim and Birkat HaMazon, even with words of Torah. One should say only these verses after mayim acharonim, before the berachah: the entire psalm "Elohim Yechoneinu Vivarcheinu" (and it is good to visualize the shape of the Menorah in one's mind), "Avarechah et Hashem bechol et" (with the intention of driving away the Sitra Achra standing at the table), "Sof davar hakol nishma," "Tehillat Hashem yedaber pi," "Va'anachnu nevarech Kah me'atah ve'ad olam, Halleluyah," and "Vayedaber elai: zeh hashulchan asher lifnei Hashem" — with intention on the final letters of this verse (zeh-hashulchan-asher), which allude to the word "NaHaR," as a further secret in the intention of the berachah. He should recite Birkat HaMazon with eyes closed as in the Amidah, left hand against the chest and right hand upon it, with intention, since the Sitra Achra stands ready to accuse if he does not bless with intention.
takeaways: One does not interrupt between mayim acharonim and the berachah, but does recite special verses
In the final verse (Vayedaber elai zeh hashulchan) one also has intention on the final letters, which allude to the secret of "NaHaR"
One recites the berachah with eyes closed and with intention, right hand upon the left against the chest

paragraphs: One should strive to recite the berachah over a cup if he has two others with him, so that they may form a zimmun (quorum for Birkat HaMazon), but one alone should not recite the berachah over a cup. Another person must hand him the cup while holding it with both hands, and likewise he should receive it with both hands; and before he says "Vayedaber elai: zeh hashulchan" and so on, he should receive the cup with both hands, and after receiving it with both hands he should hold it with the right hand alone, and then say "Vayedaber elai: zeh hashulchan" and so on, and begin to form the zimmun and recite the berachah.

clarification.explanation: One should strive to recite the berachah over a cup when there are two others with him (forming a zimmun), but one alone should not recite the berachah over a cup. Another person should hand him the cup while holding it with both hands, and the one reciting the berachah should receive it with both hands. Before saying "Vayedaber elai: zeh hashulchan" he should receive the cup with both hands, and afterward hold it with the right hand alone, and then say "Vayedaber elai: zeh hashulchan" and begin the zimmun and the berachah.
takeaways: The berachah over a cup is recited with a zimmun (three), not alone
One receives the cup with both hands, and after saying "Vayedaber elai" holds it with the right hand alone

paragraphs: The custom of the pious ones, when reciting Birkat HaMazon over a cup, is that the bread on the table be placed to the left side of the one reciting the berachah, so that the cup of blessing be in his right hand and the bread in his left; and there is a reason for this in the way of the mystical tradition.

clarification.explanation: The custom of the pious ones is that when reciting Birkat HaMazon over a cup, the bread on the table is placed to the left of the one reciting the berachah, so that the cup of blessing is in his right hand and the bread in his left, and there is a reason for this in the way of the mystical tradition.
takeaways: The bread is placed to the left of the one reciting the berachah, and the cup in his right hand
There is a mystical reason for this

paragraphs: The cup of Birkat HaMazon requires rinsing on the inside and washing on the outside, and must also be "chai" (undiluted/whole), and there are several opinions about this: some say the intention is that at the start of the berachah it should not be mixed with water, and one should only mix it in at Birkat Ha'aretz; others say the intention is that one should fill it from the flask or from the barrel for the sake of the berachah, and not from leftovers of cups; and others say the intention is that the cup be whole (undamaged). By strict law, one must be careful regarding all the reasons mentioned, to fulfill them. And after one mixes it in at Birkat Ha'aretz, it should be full, but not so full that it spills over. And after receiving it with both hands from the two hands of the one who gave it, it should remain in the right hand alone throughout the entire berachah, and the left should not assist the right. One must also raise it a handbreadth at least from the table, and keep his eyes on it throughout the entire berachah so that his mind not wander from it; and after drinking it, he should leave a little wine in it to send to his wife, even if she did not eat with him.

clarification.explanation: The cup of Birkat HaMazon requires rinsing on the inside and washing on the outside, and must be "chai" (undiluted wine). There are differing views on the meaning of "chai": some say it should not be mixed with water at the start of the berachah, only mixed in at Birkat Ha'aretz; some say it should be filled from the flask or barrel for the sake of the berachah and not from leftover cups; and some say the cup itself should be whole and undamaged. By strict law one should be careful regarding all these views. After mixing it in at Birkat Ha'aretz it should be full (but not so full that it spills), and after receiving it with both hands it should remain in the right hand alone throughout the berachah (the left should not assist), raised a handbreadth from the table, with his eyes on it throughout the berachah so his mind not wander; and after drinking, he should leave a little wine to send to his wife, even if she did not eat with him.
takeaways: The cup requires rinsing, washing, and to be "chai" (per the views: mixed only at Birkat Ha'aretz, filled fresh, whole)
Held in the right hand, raised a handbreadth, eyes kept on it, and wine left over for one's wife

paragraphs: The halachic authorities wrote that a left-handed person should take the cup in his right hand, which is the left hand of everyone else; and it appears to me, based on the mystical tradition, that even a left-handed person should take it in the right hand [of the majority of people], for the matter does not depend on the hand in this way — see Shalmei Tzibbur, page 40, halachah 14, in the name of Maharai Tzemach, of blessed memory, regarding tefillin — see there.

clarification.explanation: The halachic authorities wrote that a left-handed person should take the cup in his own right hand (which is the left hand of most people). But in Rabbeinu's view, based on the mystical tradition, even a left-handed person should take it in the right hand (the right hand of most people), since the matter does not depend specifically on this hand.
takeaways: The halachic authorities: a left-handed person takes the cup in his own right hand
Rabbeinu, based on the mystical tradition: even a left-handed person takes it in the usual right hand

paragraphs: The cup must not be defective (pagum): if one drank from it, it becomes defective, and even if one drank from the jug or from a small barrel, it becomes defective; and ab initio one must be careful even with a large barrel. And some say that even defective water is unfit to be mixed into the cup of Birkat HaMazon, and one must be careful about this.

clarification.explanation: The cup must not be defective: if one drank from it, it becomes defective, even if drunk from a jug or small barrel — one should be careful about this even ab initio with a large barrel. Some say that even defective water is unfit to be mixed into the cup of Birkat HaMazon, and one must be careful about this.
takeaways: The cup becomes defective through drinking from it (or from a jug/small barrel)
Some say even defective water is unfit to mix in

paragraphs: When he reaches Birkat Ha'aretz, saying "Uverachta et" — at the word "et" — he should mix water into it that is not defective. And it is written in Chesed LaAlafim that if the wine is strong and requires much water, and the cup must also be full, he should mix it before Birkat HaMazon so that it be full, and afterward at Birkat Ha'aretz add a little more water — see there. And it appears to me that there is room to question this, since there are those who hold that at the start of the berachah it must be "chai" (unmixed), and this reasoning appears to be primary, for the Ra'aya Meheimna states it without qualification, while the other reasonings are stated in the name of "some say"; and if he mixes it before the berachah, it turns out to be lacking "chai" according to the reasoning mentioned. Therefore, even though much water is needed and it is necessarily lacking at the start of the berachah — a deficiency noticeable to the eye — there is no problem with this, since at Birkat Ha'aretz he mixes it and it becomes full; nevertheless, it appears to me that in any case it must contain, at the start of the berachah, the measure of a revi'it.

clarification.explanation: When reaching Birkat Ha'aretz, at the word "et," he mixes the cup with water that is not defective. Chesed LaAlafim writes that if the wine is strong and requires much water, and the cup must be full, he should mix it a bit before Birkat HaMazon so it will be full, and add a little more water at Birkat Ha'aretz. But Rabbeinu questions this, since according to those who hold the cup should be "chai" (undiluted) at the start of the berachah (which appears to be the primary view), if he mixes it beforehand it will lack this condition; therefore, even though much water is needed and it will be visibly lacking at the start of the berachah, there is no problem, since it becomes full at Birkat Ha'aretz. Nevertheless, it must contain at least a revi'it at the start of the berachah.
takeaways: One mixes water into the cup at Birkat Ha'aretz, at the word "et," with water that is not defective
It is preferable to leave it "chai" (at least a revi'it) at the start and fill it at Birkat Ha'aretz

paragraphs: When he mixes the cup at Birkat Ha'aretz, he should look at the water that he pours into the cup, as our teacher, of blessed memory, wrote in Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot, Parashat Ekev, and it is explained there that the one mixing should have the intention of ninety [drops of] water, corresponding to the number of nine yuds within the four Names of Havayah of Ayin-Bet, Samech-Gimmel, Mem-Heh, and Bet-Nun — see there. And he should also be careful, when mixing, not to pour the mixing water in a single stream, but should pause the stream once or twice, so that the mixing be done in three separate pourings, one after another; so it was written in the name of Ma'avar Yabok, of blessed memory, and I wrote a reason for this in the holy work Makbetzi'el.

clarification.explanation: When mixing the cup at Birkat Ha'aretz, one should look at the water he pours into the cup, and (per the Ari) have intention that the water number ninety, corresponding to the nine yuds within the four Names of Havayah (Ayin-Bet, Samech-Gimmel, Mem-Heh, Bet-Nun). One should also be careful, when mixing, not to pour the water in a single stream, but pause once or twice, so the mixing is done in three separate pourings, one after another.
takeaways: One looks at the water while mixing and has the Ari's intention
One pours the mixing water in three separate streams, not a single stream

paragraphs: The cup of Birkat HaMazon, and likewise of Kiddush, must be whole in its rim and likewise in its base, with no defect or deficiency at all; but in a time of pressing need it is permitted. And some disqualify it even in a time of pressing need. And a crack, even without any deficiency, disqualifies — as mentioned in Chesed LaAlafim, ot dalet.

clarification.explanation: The cup of Birkat HaMazon, and likewise of Kiddush, must be whole in its rim and in its base, with no defect or deficiency at all; in a time of pressing need it is permitted to use a defective one. Some disqualify it even in a time of pressing need. And a crack — even without any deficiency — disqualifies it (Chesed LaAlafim).
takeaways: The cup for Birkat HaMazon/Kiddush must be whole in rim and base, without defect; in pressing need it is permitted (though some disqualify even then).
A crack disqualifies even without any deficiency.

paragraphs: One who is given the cup of Birkat HaMazon and does not recite the berachah — his days are shortened; nevertheless, nowadays, when the custom has spread throughout all the communities of Israel that each person recites Birkat HaMazon for himself and does not fulfill his obligation through the berachah recited by the one holding the cup — there is no concern of the kind mentioned, since each one recites the berachah himself, and consequently each and every one also blesses the host, fulfilling in him "and I will bless those who bless you," and the reason for "shortening days" is thereby nullified. But certainly one must still pursue this mitzvah even in the present time, for it is very precious, and the cup of blessing is given only to one who is generous of eye (tov ayin), who hates unjust gain and does kindness with his money, as it is said (Mishlei 22:9), "He who is generous of eye shall be blessed (yevorach)" — do not read "yevorach" but "yevarech" (he shall bless) (Sotah 38b).

clarification.explanation: One who is given the cup of Birkat HaMazon and does not recite the berachah has his days shortened. But nowadays, when the custom throughout all the communities of Israel is that each person recites Birkat HaMazon for himself and does not fulfill his obligation through the berachah of the one holding the cup, this concern does not apply, since each one blesses for himself and also blesses the host, fulfilling "and I will bless those who bless you." Nevertheless, one must certainly still pursue this precious mitzvah even nowadays. And the cup of blessing is given only to one who is "generous of eye" (tov ayin), who hates unjust gain and does kindness with his money, as it is said, "He who is generous of eye shall be blessed," and the Sages expounded: do not read "yevorach" but "yevarech" (he shall bless).
takeaways: Nowadays, since each person recites the berachah for himself, there is no concern of "shortened days"
The cup of blessing is given to one who is "generous of eye" and does kindness with his money
